headline: Exxon and Chevron Post $26.5 Billion Quarterly Profits as Drivers Pay the Price
deck: Record oil industry profits arrive at the pump with sticker shock as geopolitical tensions and Wall Street disappointment collide.
body: ExxonMobil and Chevron banked $26.5 billion in combined profits for the quarter, the latest windfall from a global oil market roiled by US-Iran tensions. The earnings, revealed Tuesday, mark the highest quarterly take for the American oil majors in years, even as Exxon missed profit estimates despite hitting a four-year high. Drivers filling their tanks this week are paying the direct cost—gasoline prices have surged, leaving consumers to absorb the squeeze.

Exxon’s quarterly profits reached levels unseen since 2020, but the company still fell short of Wall Street’s expectations, sending its stock down 1.8% in after-hours trading. Analysts point to the gap between soaring revenues and investor demands as a sign of lingering discontent with capital discipline. Meanwhile, Chevron posted stronger-than-expected earnings, underscoring the uneven performance within the sector.

The rise in oil prices has been fueled by escalating tensions between the US and Iran, which have disrupted shipping lanes and raised fears of supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude hit $92 a barrel last month, its highest level since last autumn, and shows no sign of retreating. Analysts at The New York Times called it “the highest levels in years,” a phrase now echoed across energy desks.

The human cost is visible at gas stations from Houston to Hialeah, where drivers are trading smaller tanks for bigger financial pain. The Washington Post reported widespread “sticker shock” as commuters and small businesses recalibrate budgets already strained by inflation. One Virginia driver told the paper, “I used to fill up for $40. Now it’s $80. And I’m the same guy doing the same job.”

The political fallout is immediate. Former President Donald Trump criticized the oil companies in a Truth Social post Tuesday night, writing, “These greedy oil companies are making billions while families pay the price.” His statement echoed broader public frustration, with polls showing energy costs now rivaling healthcare and housing as top voter concerns ahead of the election.

Exxon’s miss on estimates—despite revenue jumping 32% year-over-year—highlights a disconnect between revenue growth and investor confidence. Reuters noted that refining margins weakened in the quarter, offsetting gains from higher crude prices. The company said it would return $17.5 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks, a move likely to appease some critics but not all.

Across the industry, profits are being described as a “windfall” by energy analysts. OilPrice.com called the quarter “a stark contrast between company balance sheets and household budgets,” noting that while share prices rose, consumer pain deepened. The AP framed it bluntly: “Major oil companies reap massive profits as US and Iran fighting drives energy prices higher.”

Political and consumer backlash is coalescing. While oil companies defend their earnings as a result of market forces, critics argue that record profits amid rising costs reveal a structural imbalance. The White House has so far avoided direct criticism of the companies, instead blaming global instability and calling for strategic petroleum reserve releases. But with gasoline prices now a top political liability, pressure is building fast.
